claims.claim: In its prescriptive political usage, 'equality' is a highly contested concept: people who praise or disparage it disagree about what it requires.

The formal principle of equality, often traced to Aristotle, requires treating like cases alike; it does not by itself specify which respects are normatively relevant, and it is interpreted either as a rule of rationality or as a moral principle of justice.

Formal equality of opportunity holds that positions and advantages should be open to all and allocated by open, merit-based competition, with no legal or coercive barriers; it does not address background conditions that affect who can become qualified.

Fair equality of opportunity, as formulated by John Rawls, requires that people with the same level of talent and ability and the same willingness to use them have the same prospects of success regardless of their social class of origin.

Most contemporary egalitarians do not advocate equality of outcome; they defend different forms of equality of opportunity, partly because of the moral significance they attach to individual responsibility for choices.

Amartya Sen pioneered the capabilities approach, which evaluates well-being in terms of people's real freedoms to achieve functionings (doings and beings); Sen argues that equal resources can yield unequal capabilities because people differ in converting resources into functionings, as illustrated by his example of two persons with identical resources, one of whom has a disability.

Egalitarian, sufficiency, and priority views answer the question of what distribution should be sought differently: egalitarianism treats equality itself as valuable, the sufficiency view (Frankfurt 1987) holds that what matters is that each person has enough, and the priority view (Parfit 1997) holds that benefiting people matters more the worse off they are.

The leveling-down objection, associated with Derek Parfit, charges that a policy which reduces inequality by making the better-off worse off without benefiting anyone is intuitively objectionable; egalitarians respond that equality can be intrinsically valuable, and some note contexts, such as positional goods, where leveling down may be less objectionable.

Feminist critics of purely procedural equality argue that equal treatment may require taking relevant differences into account: liberal feminists hold that like cases should be treated alike, while 'difference' feminists such as Martha Minow argue that equality requires attending to physical, historical, and social differences, giving rise to 'dilemmas of difference'.

Disability-focused critiques of formal equality hold that identical treatment can fail people who are differently situated, since equal resources may not convert into equal capabilities for people with disabilities; the capability literature presents disability as a conversion factor that resource-based metrics miss.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether equality of outcome is morally objectionable when it requires leveling down.
positions: Critics such as Parfit argue that a distribution made equal by worsening the position of the better-off without benefiting anyone is intuitively objectionable, suggesting that priority rather than equality is the underlying value.
Egalitarians respond that equality can be intrinsically valuable, that equality may be balanced against other values, and that for positional goods leveling down may be appropriate (Temkin).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the leveling-down objection and the egalitarian responses as an open philosophical debate and does not adjudicate it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether equal treatment requires identical treatment.
positions: Procedural or formal views hold that like cases should be treated alike, leaving open which respects are relevant.
Difference-focused feminists (Minow) and capability theorists argue that ignoring relevant differences can perpetuate disadvantage, so equal treatment may require different treatment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both positions are presented neutrally as rival answers to the question of what equality requires.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What should be equalized: resources, welfare, or capabilities.
positions: Resource egalitarians focus on equal holdings of resources such as income and wealth.
Welfare egalitarians focus on equal well-being or preference satisfaction, facing the expensive-tastes problem.
Capability theorists (Sen, Nussbaum) focus on real freedoms to achieve functionings.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the metric question as contested and attributes each view; it does not select a winner.

sourceRecords.title: Equality (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21 (entry by Richard J. Arneson, substantive revision 2021). Supports: equality as a contested concept; the formal equality principle 'treat like cases as like' attributed to Aristotle and its rationality (Berlin) vs moral-principle readings; equality of welfare vs equality of resources; Sen's capabilities approach as an alternative metric; the claim that most egalitarians favor equality of opportunity over equality of outcome; the sufficiency view (Frankfurt 1987) and the priority view (Parfit 1997). Reference only; all lesson prose is original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Equality of Opportunity (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports the distinctions among formal equality of opportunity (advantages open to all; no legal or coercive restrictions; meritocratic selection), substantive equality of opportunity (addressing background obstacles to becoming qualified, including the Bernard Williams warrior-class illustration), and Rawls's fair equality of opportunity (equal talent and willingness yield equal prospects regardless of social class of origin). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Egalitarianism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports the leveling-down objection (Parfit 1997: removing resources from the better-off until they are as badly off as the worst-off seems intuitively objectionable), the associated move from equality to priority, and egalitarian responses (equality as intrinsically valuable; Temkin 2000 on positional goods and contexts where leveling down may be less objectionable). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: The Capability Approach (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21 (entry by Ingrid Robeyns). Supports: Amartya Sen as the pioneer of the capability approach (developed further by Martha Nussbaum and others); functionings as doings and beings and capabilities as real freedoms to achieve them; Sen's 'Equality of What?' (1979) example of two persons with identical resources where one has a disability; conversion factors as enabling and disabling conditions; the approach's attention to human diversity, relevant to feminist and disability critiques. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Feminist Philosophy of Law (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Section 1.4 'Equality and Difference' supports: liberal feminist procedural equality ('like cases should be treated alike and different cases differently in proportion to their differences') and the observation that procedural equality leaves open which respects are relevant; difference feminists (Minow 1990) holding that equality requires taking physical, historical, social, and other significant differences into account; Minow's 'dilemmas of difference' (taking a difference into account can seem required for equality yet also appear to instantiate inequality). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Egalitarianism (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Tier B cross-check. Supports: formal equality of opportunity as open meritocratic competition that prohibits allocating positions on the basis of gender, ethnicity, and similar traits, and substantive equality of opportunity as additionally addressing the preparation of candidates; the leveling-down objection and the strict-egalitarian response that equality may be intrinsically valuable; the contrast between views that prioritize the worst off or guarantee a sufficient minimum and those that pursue strict equality; welfare vs resource metrics including the expensive-tastes problem and disability as inefficiency in welfare generation. Reference only.
